item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are National League West champions for the 13th time in the last 14 seasons, and the fifth consecutive year.
More than half of their reign over the division has coincided with Mookie Betts’ tenure with the franchise. Betts now has been part of six Dodgers teams that have won the NL West, and of course three World Series championships as well.
“It’s amazing,” Betts told David Vassegh on SportsNet LA when discussing the 2026 NL West title. “Obviously it’s not just me. We’ve got a great group of guys. It’s fun. Step one. We’ve got a long way to go, but winning is always fun.”
Mookie Betts makes promise
Part of the Dodgers’ success this year, especially over the past several weeks, has come because of Betts improving on season-long struggles.
“Thank you for sticking with me,” Betts said when asked if he had a message for Dodgers fans. “I know it was hard. I make it hard sometimes, but thank you for sticking by my side, by our side. We’ve got something special coming.”
With a 14th consecutive postseason berth on the horizon, the Dodgers are still playing for seeding in the NL bracket. Scenarios still open to them range from the No. 1 seed to being third. They enter play Friday trailing the Milwaukee Brewers by two games for the best record in baseball.
At No. 2 in the NL, the Dodgers are four games ahead of the Atlanta Braves for the all-important bye in the first round of the postseason. L.A. does not hold the tiebreaker over the Brewers or Braves.
With respect to Atlanta, the Dodgers missed out on an opportunity to clinch the tiebreaker due to getting swept at Truist Park from Aug. 25-27. Though, the implications and potential playoff preview did not resonate with Betts.
“We’ve won two Wild Card Series, we’ve won with the bye. So I don’t think it really matters,” Betts said of NL seeding during that series. “I mean, if you want to make it matter, sure. But it doesn’t matter when you play. You’re going to have to get timely hits and pitch. There’s no secret or magic formula to it. It’s just about playing good ball.”

The Los Angeles Dodgers remain the cream of the crop in MLB, as their consistency year after year is something to behold. On Thursday, the Dodgers sealed the inevitable, winning their 13th NL West title in 14 seasons, with an 8-2 victory on the road against the Cincinnati Reds, giving them a 93-60 record on the season thus far.
LA has won everything there is to win over the past decade or so, but winning a division title is never easy even though they've made it look like it, making it a cause for celebration every single time. But the Dodgers, having won so much already, have to spice up their celebrations from time to time the way utility man Kike Hernandez did on Thursday.
Hernandez, during the Dodgers' champagne-popping celebration in the locker room, was caught on camera pouring a bottle of champagne down the shorts of ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Yamamoto appeared to be caught off guard by this wild act from his teammate, and he tried his best afterwards to remove the bottle that Hernandez put inside his shorts.

Hernandez has already won three World Series titles with the Dodgers, so he certainly is no stranger to some out of pocket scenes in the locker room during this sort of celebration. But it's a testament to how close this team is and how comfortable they are with each other that Hernandez can get away with such a wild act that is, of course, all in jest.
Both Hernandez and Yamamoto have been postseason heroes for the Dodgers, with the former starring for them in 2024 and latter pitching his heart out last year. They have already shown that they have the clutch gene, so when the dust settles on this celebration, fans can be certain that both of them will lock in as well as they proceed in their quest to win three consecutive World Series titles.

CINCINNATI -- Try as they might to view 2026 as its own season, everything the Dodgers have done this year is impossible to separate from the larger context of what they have accomplished in more than a decade of excellence.
The Dodgers hit another key milestone in their title defense by reclaiming the NL West crown with an 8-2 victory over the Reds on Thursday afternoon at Great American Ball Park. Three days after their traditional champagne toast in honor of clinching a postseason berth, winning the West brought on a wild clubhouse celebration -- which they hope will be the first of many over the next several weeks.
"You get so mired in each year, it’s hard to have any perspective," president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said. "We’ve had our share of troubles this year. Things where we had to work harder than we expected on a couple of fronts. But the important thing is how we finish and how we go into October."
In their record-tying 14 consecutive postseason appearances, the Dodgers have 13 division titles. The only team to unseat them was the 2021 Giants, who edged them in one of the most highly contested NL West races in recent memory.
Since divisional play began in 1969, the Dodgers lead all big league teams with 24 division titles, one more than the Braves -- currently in line to win the NL East -- and three more than the Yankees. Each year's achievements raise the bar for every ensuing year. The expectations facing the Dodgers have become nearly impossible to meet. But they've embraced them gladly.
"There is certainly a higher expectation when, if you don't win the World Series, you fail," manager Dave Roberts said. "But that's kind of part of what you signed up with the Dodgers.”
The Dodgers' offense, whose inconsistency has been a perpetual concern over the course of the season, provided plenty of early support to back a scheduled bullpen game. Kyle Tucker led the way with a four-hit, three-RBI showing, finishing a triple shy of the Dodgers’ first cycle since 2017. Freddie Freeman, Max Muncy, Josue De Paula and Miguel Rojas also knocked in runs.
Justin Wrobleski opened the bullpen game with three perfect innings, and while Blake Treinen surrendered a solo home run in the fourth, Landon Knack pitched four scoreless frames before Seth Halvorsen allowed a run in the ninth.
With nine games remaining in the regular season, the Dodgers are far from full strength. Their best hitter, Shohei Ohtani, is on the 15-day IL, as is first-time All-Star Andy Pages. The six-man rotation they carried for most of the season has been reduced to four fully stretched-out starters on the active roster, necessitating Thursday's bullpen game.
"It's been the same thing the last couple years," Muncy said. "We've had guys go down. We've had guys step up in their place. … That's all that we ask, and we've been able to survive a lot."
The Dodgers are expecting reinforcements back before the postseason, and would greatly benefit from securing a first-round bye to advance directly to the NL Division Series -- giving them five days off after the end of the regular season. They hold a four-game lead over the Braves for the No. 2 seed in the National League.
This edition of the Dodgers is not without its flaws, but then again, neither were the back-to-back champion teams in 2024 and '25. After becoming the first team in a quarter-century to defend their title last year, they will vie for the Majors' first three-peat since the 1998-2000 Yankees.
While the talk of a three-peat began almost from the moment the Dodgers became back-to-back champions last November, Roberts urged his team to stay focused on the present while keeping the larger goal in mind. In his annual speech on the first day of full-squad workouts during Spring Training, he delivered the following message: Be a greyhound, looking forward with blinders on.
Tarik Skubal was not a Dodger when Roberts gave his spring address, but he saw the message play out after he was dealt to L.A. ahead of the Trade Deadline. He arrived at the beginning of a season-high seven-game losing streak -- and the tough stretch gave him a feel for the culture that has led to his new team's sustained success.
"I think there was no panic from this group," Skubal said. "I think that’s why in big moments, pressure doesn't really get to these guys."
The Dodgers have a long road ahead as they look to get back to the World Series, but it bears similarities to the roads they have traveled before. The slate might be wiped clean every year, but they have experience weathering the challenges along the way to the promised land.
"It's a different year, but I think it's kind of the same," Mookie Betts said. "The same group of guys. We know what to expect. We know what to expect from each other. It's the same goal every year. Getting here, you can't really get too focused on how, as long as you get there."

"Being on a winning team, I live for those special moments. I can't wait until we start winning in the playoffs. It's going to be cool."

Los Dodgers de Los Ángeles aseguraron su quinto título consecutivo de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional y el 13.º en las últimas 14 temporadas al vencer el jueves 8-2 a los Rojos de Cincinnati.
"Es algo muy importante. Creo que mucha gente piensa que es solo un rito de paso (pero) no es fácil", declaró el mánager de los Dodgers Dave Roberts. "Así que es algo de lo que todos estamos muy orgullosos, pero entendemos claramente que ese no es el objetivo final".
Los Dodgers (93-60) disputarán los playoffs por 14.ª temporada consecutiva, con lo que igualan el récord que los Bravos de Atlanta establecieron de 1991-2005.
"Es el primer paso", dijo Mookie Betts mientras se secaba el champán de los ojos. "Nos queda un largo camino por recorrer".
La celebración en el terreno de juego fue algo calmada tras el último out el jueves. Pero los jugadores se soltaron en el vestuario, donde el champán y la cerveza salpicaron desde el suelo hasta el techo.
"Creo que es una de esas situaciones en las que, como en el béisbol se juega a diario, los jugadores se centran en rendir", dijo Roberts. "Así que no hay muchos momentos para celebrar. Por eso es agradable ver a los chicos soltarse un poco".
A pesar de todos sus laureles, los Dodgers creen que todavía tienen algo que demostrar.
El año pasado, el equipo pulverizó el récord de gasto de las Grandes Ligas con una nómina total de 515 millones de dólares, dando alas a críticas de que tienen una supuesta ventaja injusta.
"Lo que estamos creando aquí es especial", afirmó Max Muncy. "Definitivamente no se le da el reconocimiento que merece. Todo el mundo se fija en la nómina, pero nunca hablamos de cómo hacemos las cosas bien, de cómo nos preparamos adecuadamente o de cómo cuidamos todos esos pequeños detalles. De eso no se habla".
Los bicampeones defensores de la Serie Mundial aún pujan por el primer puesto de preclasificación de la Liga Nacional, que actualmente está en posesión de los Cerveceros de Milwaukee. Los Ángeles comenzó el día con una ventaja de tres juegos y medio sobre los Bravos (89-64) por el segundo puesto, pero está por detrás de los Cerveceros (95-57).
"Seguimos luchando por uno de los dos primeros puestos", dijo Roberts. "Creo que hacemos bien celebrando, pero sin dejar que eso afecte a lo que sigue. Tenemos que tomar el vuelo y jugar contra los Gigantes mañana".
Los Dodgers buscan convertirse en el primer equipo en conquistar tres campeonatos consecutivos de la Serie Mundial desde que los Yankees lo lograron de 1998 a 2000.
Este es el cuarto título divisional asegurado más temprano para los Dodgers. Aseguraron el Oeste de la Liga Nacional el 10 de septiembre de 2019, el 13 de septiembre de 2022 y el 16 de septiembre de 2023.
Los Ángeles aprovechará ese tiempo para recuperar lesionados. Eso empieza con Shohei Ohtani.
El cuatro veces Jugador Más Valioso ha estado en la lista de lesionados de 15 días desde el 8 de septiembre por una inflamación en el bíceps derecho y les dijo a los reporteros a principios de este mes que ya no lanzará más en lo que resta de temporada. La estrella de dos vías hizo swings desde un tee por primera vez el martes y se sintió bien. Se espera que regrese como bateador antes de que termine la temporada regular, aunque no está claro si podrá llegar al 100 % de salud antes de octubre.
Roki Sasaki, en la lista de lesionados por una ampolla en el dedo medio, lanzó en una práctica de bateo en vivo el miércoles en Cincinnati y salió bien. Roberts indicó que su próxima aparición será como abridor.
Blake Snell salió prematuramente de la apertura del miércoles después de un inning por rigidez en la ingle izquierda. Su situación es incierta.
Se espera que el cerrador puertorriqueño Edwin Díaz, quien ha estado en la lista de lesionados desde agosto por una inflamación en el cuello, sea activado el viernes. El venezolano Edgardo Henríquez, un preparador de mesa en el bullpen, está en la lista de lesionados por molestias en la parte baja de la espalda. Se le realizó una resonancia magnética en Los Ángeles el miércoles, que reveló una distensión lumbar, y su rehabilitación se pausará por unos días.
El primera base Freddie Freeman, aquejado por dolor en la rodilla derecha, regresó a la alineación el martes y cortó una mala racha de 3 hits en 30 turnos con tres imparables. Sumó otros dos hits el jueves.
Los Dodgers protagonizaron el mayor impacto de la fecha límite de cambios al adquirir a Tarik Skubal, ganador en dos ocasiones del premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, procedente de los Tigres. Skubal tiene marca de 3-2 con efectividad de 2.52 en ocho aperturas con los Dodgers.
La incorporación de Skubal convirtió a los Dodgers en los grandes favoritos en las apuestas para ganar la Serie Mundial. Pero después de comenzar la temporada con marca de 61-36, los Dodgers tienen registro de 31-24 desde la pausa del Juego de Estrellas.
Los Dodgers dejaron a 12 corredores en base y se fueron de 0 en 11 con corredores en posición de anotar en la derrota del miércoles ante los Reds, algo que, según Roberts, necesita mejorar.
"Se trata de poder rematar a los equipos cuando tenemos oportunidades. En la postemporada no se presentan muchas oportunidades. Hay que saber aprovecharlas", dijo Roberts.

Mookie Betts has a message for Los Angeles Dodgers fans following Thursday’s win over the Cincinnati Reds, which clinched the Dodgers’ fifth straight National League West title after a tumultuous season for the 33-year-old shortstop.
Betts entered Thursday’s game batting .250 with a .316 on-base percentage and a 103 OPS+, well off his career norms. He had 20 home runs with 62 RBIs in 114 games this season, missing time with an oblique strain and facing criticism from parts of the fan base during his early slump, which even led him to step away from social media in May.

Tarik Skubal is 29 years old.

Los Angeles Dodgers shortstop Mookie Betts thanked fans for their support as he battled a hitting slump and injuries again this year.
After the Dodgers clinched the National League West on Thursday, September 17th, Betts reflected on his regular season thus far, which has featured a bumpy ride.
“Thank you for sticking with me. I know it was hard. I make it hard sometimes, but thank you for sticking by my side. By our side. We’ve got something special coming,” Betts said as champagne poured on his face.
This season, Betts battled an oblique injury that sidelined him for about a month, and he started the season poorly at the plate.
In the first month of late March and April, Betts had a 95 wRC+ and a .710 OPS. Then, things got worse until May, with a 75 wRC+ and a .650 OPS.
Things picked up in June, with a 122 wRC+, but July and the first half of August were rough again.
Now, Betts is helping to give the team a last-minute spark.
Mookie Betts’ recent turnaround
Betts has really turned it on offensively over the last month, hitting .280/.366/.466 with five home runs and 23 RBIs.
Along with his standout defense at such a highly valuable position at shortstop, Betts has not been a superstar this year, but instead has been a very good player.
He has a 2.8 fWAR, with a 1.4 offensive rating and a 10.5 defensive rating, both above average, per FanGraphs.
More than the results, he is hitting the ball hard and commanding the strike zone well.
The arrow is pointing up for Mookie Betts at the right time.

They hit their magic number, but minus the magic.
The Dodgers trudged toward October by clinching their 13th National League West title in 14 years on Thursday, their customary march mired in a quicksand of questions.
Has any Dodger team during this golden era entered the playoffs with more injuries, more uncertainty, and a greater fear of underachievement?
Will the party in Cincinnati be the last time they celebrate this season?
The magic is indeed missing, and after two seasons of conjuring up postseason greatness, these back-to-reality Dodgers appear headed for an early fall.
The Three-Peat looks like a no-go.
Despite the best efforts from baseball’s best braintrust, their latest creation simply doesn’t have the appearance of a championship team.
They’re aging, they’re hurting and, with only a couple of weeks left until the beginning of their annual autumnal angst, they look tired and taut and unprepared for this monumental tussle with history.
“I think for me, the message was, ‘We haven’t come close to playing our best baseball yet.’” manager Dave Roberts told reporters when relaying his speech to the team earlier this week upon clinching a record-tying 14th consecutive playoff berth.
He added, “The message was, we’ve accomplished a lot up to this point, all the while not playing our best baseball. So let’s get some of these guys healthy.”
Haven’t come close to playing our best baseball… Let’s get some of these guys healthy.
Not exactly “Win one for the Gipper” stuff, but completely accurate. These postseason’s themes are more realistic than inspirational, and for good reason.
No, they haven’t come close to playing their best baseball. Forget what you see in these season-ending games against some of the worst teams. Remember, instead, what they’ve done against some of baseball’s best.
Since the All-Star break, they are 4-12 against the five National League playoff contenders. The Atlanta Braves swept them. The Chicago Cubs swept them. The Milwaukee Brewers dominated them.
These teams will be waiting for them in October, and even baseball’s richest roster might not be enough to carry this staggered bunch through their toughest stretch. They’ve played a lot of games in three years, all under baseball’s brightest spotlight, every night, scores of media, millions of fans, a worldwide whirl for 28 regular dudes, and it’s finally taken its toll.
They’ve hit the wall… and the wall is about to hit back.
“It’s not easy, I think it’s a lot harder than people think it is,” said Roberts. “Human nature alone, when you’re hungry, when you’re chasing something, it’s a lot more easy to be motivated, versus, having been there, done that, it gets a little trite, a little old.”
He added: “To keep guys enthusiastic, focused, hungry, that’s harder. But to their credit, they stayed the course. And for me, we’re just as hungry as we were in ‘24 and ‘25. This is a separate season. Our guys understand.”
The 1988-89 Lakers understood, too. And they still got burned in ways that Dodger fans will find painfully familiar. Showtime was chasing the original “three-peat” trademarked by Pat Riley when the Lakers were swept by the Detroit Pistons in a Finals that seemed cursed,
Byron Scott missed the series with a hamstring injury and Magic Johnson essentially missed the final two games with a hamstring injury and they couldn’t survive.
This looks like the Dodgers today. Their injuries feel too major, and the impact too deep.
Start with Shohei Ohtani. The Dodgers haven’t won a full-season championship in 38 years without him at the top of the lineup. He’ll be there again, but his body has been breaking down for the last couple of months, and, before being recently placed on the injured list — finally! — he was only a shadow of himself.
He hasn’t hit a home run or driven in a run outside of Coors Field in more than a month. In his last 24 games before going on the IL with biceps and knee issues, he was batting .198. The Dodgers can’t admit it, and Ohtani would never acknowledge it, but this is a man in serious need of an extended rest.
Teoscar Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday in the Dodgers’ win against the Reds was his second home run in as many nights.
Also on the injured list in these final days is Andy Pages, who was having a career year before breaking his hand. He’ll return without much time to get ready for October, and this is a man who will need some time, as he has a career .114 average in the postseason and was even benched last year before he redeemed himself with that picturesque catch over Kiké Hernández.
Speaking of last October’s heroes, the biggest savior has also spent the summer in pain, Will Smith battling neck issues until recently returning to the lineup. But the comeback has been bumpy. In his initial games since returning at the start of September, Smith was batting .171. Last October he set a major league record by catching 73 innings in the World Series. He is still paying the price.
Then there’s Freddie Freeman, whose bat doesn’t have the same pop, who’s step doesn’t have the same spring, and who has his worst OPS in 14 years. Add an inconsistent Mookie Betts and an incredibly streaky Teoscar Hernández to an already-shaky lineup.
It’s been such an unsteady year, Andrew Friedman’s two big offseason acquisitions have been busts. Edwin Díaz has been terrible, and then injured, then terrible again. Kyle Tucker has been terrible, then worse, then mostly invisible.
Even the Dodgers two role-playing heroes have seemingly disappeared. Kiké Hernández, at age 35, has his lowest home-run total — three — in 12 years. Miguel Rojas, at age 37, has his lowest home run and RBI totals in nine years.
The Dodgers clinch a playoff berth with their 4-1 victory over the Cincinnati Reds, reaching the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year.
As if they didn’t have enough problems on the field and at the plate, check out the mound. No, don’t.
Even what should be their strength is now being threatened. Blake Snell left Wednesday’s game early with groin issues and Tyler Glasnow recently complained of general discomfort. This leaves a proven playoff rotation of two, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tarik Skubal, and if you think Yamamoto threw a lot of innings last October, this time he won’t be able to leave the mound for a month.
In all, this is a Dodger team facing its toughest challenge yet, their quest for an historic three-peat much tougher than the last two journeys, one that will require arguably the greatest stretch of baseball in franchise history to complete.
This division title is a nice beginning.
It could also be the end.

Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal was spotted doing Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s signature workout ahead of the team’s game vs. the Reds.
Skubal has been on the team for only a month or so, but he seems to be taking a liking to his fellow starters.
On Thursday, September 17th, Skubal was spotted with Yamamoto and his translator, throwing the javelin, a staple of the Japanese star.
Yamamoto has been one of the more unique minds when it comes to his preparation, using a ton of flexibility and motion techniques.
This is not the first sign of Skubal’s appreciation for Yamamoto. When he first joined the team, Skubal was impressed with Yamamoto right off the bat.
“Yoshi’s process is nuts too, you know. I think that what he does is insane too, and watching his bullpens, the preparation is second to none,” Skubal told Dodgers Nation.
Why does Yamamoto throw javelins?
His famous javelin toss is just one part of a routine created by personal trainer Osamu Yada, who started working with Yamamoto during his teenage years in Japan.
Since then, “Yada Sensei,” as he is referred to, has worked with other members of the Dodgers, including Mookie Betts over the spring.
“I’m not fully in his whole routine,” Betts said of Yada. “But I wake up every morning and do my stretch routine that Sensei showed me, throwing the javelins every day.
“I think throwing javelins is the reason why I can make a play in the hole like that and throw it in the air on a line. I’m really grateful for Yoshi and Sensei, because they have definitely changed my perspective, changed my life, changed my game.”
Yamamoto has credited these workouts as the main reason the Dodgers’ ace can pitch often and, thus far, avoid serious injuries.
If the javelin can help Skubal as well, Yada Sensei’s legend will only grow.

The Los Angeles Dodgers brought third baseman Max Muncy and outfielder Josue De Paula back into the lineup for Thursday’s series finale against the Cincinnati Reds.
The Dodgers lost Wednesday’s game after Cy Young winner Blake Snell went down with a groin injury after pitching just one inning. Luckily, Snell believes he can still make a start before the end of the regular season, which ends in less than two weeks.
LA won the first two games of the series, shutting down a powerful Reds lineup, and will look to do the same to win the series Wednesday.
Who is Starting for the Dodgers?
Justin Wrobleski will start for the Dodgers on Wednesday, making his 25th appearance of the regular season. Two of his last three appearances have come out of the bullpen, and none of them have lasted more than three innings since his return from the injured list with a forearm problem.
He has a 3.78 ERA on the year, striking out 111 batters over the course of 133.1 innings—his heaviest workload in an MLB season so far.
How deep into the game he goes depends on him, but the Dodgers will have backup in the form of Landon Knack whenever Wrobleski is ready to come out.
Who is in the Dodgers’ Lineup?
The Dodgers still don’t have Shohei Ohtani in the lineup, but Tommy Edman has replaced him well and will play center field on Thursday. Freddie Freeman moves up a couple of spots into the No. 2 hole, followed by right fielder Kyle Tucker, who will bat third.
Left fielder Teoscar Hernandez takes over the cleanup spot, followed by Muncy, who slides back into third base and bats fifth. De Paula serves as the designated hitter and will bat sixth, with catcher Hunter Feduccia giving Will Smith an off day in the No. 7 spot.
Second baseman Alex Freeland will bat eight for the Dodgers, with Miguel Rojas rounding out the lineup and playing shortstop—giving Mookie Betts a well-deserved rest day.

Who is Starting for the Reds?
Veteran right-hander Brady Singer is starting for the Reds, making his 30th appearance of the season. He has reached that mark in each of the last three seasons, and has 25 or more appearances in all seven of his MLB campaigns bar 2020.
He isn’t having the best year despite his regular consistency, though, as he has a 5.38 ERA through 150.2 innings with only 125 strikeouts on the season.
Singer didn’t face the Dodgers in last week’s series in Los Angeles, but he has a pretty good track record against the team. In three appearances against LA, all of which came during his time with Kansas City, he has a 1.89 ERA through 19 innings with 15 strikeouts.
The Dodgers will hope to break that trend on Thursday as they look to bring themselves even closer to a first-round postseason bye. The first pitch of Thursday’s game comes at 9:40 p.m. PT.

The Los Angeles Dodgers lost to the Cincinnati Reds, 6-2, on Wednesday and fell to 92-60 on the year.
Blake Snell pitched just one inning before he was removed from his start due to groin tightness. After Blake Treinen pitched a clean second inning, the Reds took advantage of the impromptu bullpen game and halted any potential NL West-clinching celebrations.
Offensively, Mookie Betts still shined with a three-hit outing and Will Smith also enjoyed a multi-hit night. The backstop appears to be gaining his footing once again, hitting .273 with three RBIs in his last seven games.
Ahead of the eventual defeat, the Dodgers surprisingly designated an outfielder for assignment hitting .218 in his first 20 MLB games in order to make room on the roster to activate All-Star right-hander Kris Bubic. Though it wasn't the most ideal situation to be making his debut with the two-time defending champions, Bubic struck out two in a scoreless eighth inning.
After the game, both Snell and manager Dave Roberts provided an update on the left-hander's injury. Snell revealed that he felt his groin "grab" during a pregame bullpen and knew then he shouldn't go beyond the first inning. Regardless, he said he "should be good" to make another start before the postseason.
Roberts, however, wasn't as sure.
“It’s a possibility,” Roberts said. “I like where his head is at, but he just can’t afford any more setbacks. So, whether it’s his next start or being pushed back or whatever it is, we’ve got to make sure that he comes out ready to go in the postseason.”
Finally, right-hander and presumed closer Edwin Díaz doesn't appear to be making much progress amid his return from another injured list stint. Manager Dave Roberts, among others, was not happy with the results of his rehab outing over the weekend, and knows that at this moment, Díaz is not someone a World Series favorite wants in their bullpen this postseason.
Díaz had a slightly better outing Wednesday (one scoreless inning) after his disastrous Sunday performance of five earned runs in 0.2 innings.

Dodgers catcher Will Smith was the team's nominee for the 2026 Roberto Clemente Award, the annual honor that recognizes players for their contributions both on and off the field, named for the legendary Hall of Fame former Pittsburgh Pirates outfielder.
Smith and his wife Cara founded Catching Hope, "a nonprofit organization working to help underprivileged children with critical skills needed for leadership, self-advocacy, and self-sufficiency." Among the projects by the organization this year include an art installation at Marquez Elementary School in Los Angeles in April, a comedy night in Beverly Hills in May as part of the Netflix is a Joke Fest, a community clinic for an elementary school at Dodger Stadium in May, and a visit to UCLA hospital in August.

— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) August 17, 2026
Fans can vote on the Clemente Award through September 27, the final day of the regular season. The fan vote will count as one vote in a panel that also includes members of the MLB commissioner's office, MLB.com writers, MLB television media partners, and members of Roberto Clemente's family.
The winner will be announced during the World Series. Dodgers shortstop Mookie Betts won the award last year.
Old friend Justin Turner, who won the Clemente Award in 2022 and was also the Dodgers nominee for the honor in 2017, 2018, 2020, and 2021 as well, won another title on Tuesday night. His Tijuana Toros beat the Tabasco Olmecas four games to two to win the best-of-7 Serie del Rey to win the Mexican League championship.

It’s led by founder and CEO Diego Torres-Palma and James Beard Award-winning chef Tony Messina. Together they’ve made the standard sports bar menu of chicken wings, nachos and mozzarella sticks look insulting by comparison.
A housemade wagyu hot dog, beef tallow fries, chicken liver mousse, caviar and charbroiled Maine oysters are just some of the menu’s highlights.

It’s who is behind it.
Billionaire entrepreneur and former Dallas Mavericks owner Mark Cuban is an investor. So is Dodgers’ president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman.
The list of names interested in either investing or being a part of the business is longer than a CVS receipt.
“We literally traded emails when Aaron announced he was coming back,” Torres-Palma said.
Donald isn’t the only Dodgers-or-Rams-adjacent star circling the new sports bar. Dodgers’ shortstop Mookie Betts met with the company and will now feature his Tequila Providencia behind the bar. Torres-Palma said Providencia’s CEO Rodd Rafieha’s tequila impressed his beverage team enough to earn a place in the well.
Kendall Jenner’s 818 Tequila also wanted in on the fun.
“We’re excited to have 818 Tequila featured at Pawn Shop LA,” said Lanay Jacobs, President of 818 Tequila. “It’s a lively destination that brings together sports, cocktails, and community in a way our audience will love.”
Torres-Palma has other meetings set up with L.A. superstar athletes as well.
That collection of names helps explain why Pawn Shop has quickly become less a sports bar and more a hangout spot for athletes and celebrities alike.
Former NBA player Chandler Parsons, now the co-host of the online show “Run It Back,” makes a point to stop by at least once a week.
“Pawn Shop is exactly what LA needed,” he said. “Great food, great energy, amazing people, and a genuine love for sports that you can feel when you walk in.”
Sportscaster and radio host Rich Eisen recently held his fantasy football draft there. The entire LAFC team did the same. Actor Anthony Ramos has stopped by several times. Several entertainment executives have used the space, while nearby Paramount staffers have turned its private upstairs suites into off-site work rooms.
Cuban recently visited with his son and was in awe.
“Of all the investors, Mark is probably the one that I communicate with the most,” Torres-Palma said. “He’s so pumped. Honestly, he’s probably been our top supporter.”
The timing of Pawn Shop’s opening could hardly have been better.
It arrived during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, instantly giving an unknown sports bar the kind of crowds and atmosphere most restaurants spend years trying to manufacture.
Torres-Palma compares those first weeks to hosting a wedding every few days: hundreds of customers arriving together, watching the same event and wanting food and drinks at virtually the same moment.
The peak came during Mexico’s wild Round of 16 match against England.
“I’ll never forget the roars in here,” Torres-Palma said. “That feeling is why you build these things. It’s such a crazy, loud, energetic feeling that everybody experiences at the same time.”
He even has a phrase for it: “monetizing moments.”
It sounds cold until you stand inside a room filled with hundreds of strangers collectively losing their minds over a goal. When fans of El Tri or the Three Lions look back on that historic match, they’ll remember being at Pawn Shop and sharing a memory they’ll never forget with others.
That’s what “monetizing moments” is all about. It’s also a pretty good description of the entire sports business.
The question now is whether Pawn Shop can sustain that feeling now that the World Cup is over.
Los Angeles is littered with restaurants that were once the hottest reservation in town. Sports bars and national chains have closed locations, too. Novelty disappears quickly here.
“When people say the restaurant business is brutal or very tough, I always ask them, ‘What’s an easy business so I can go do that?’” he said.
His answer to struggling competitors is considerably sharper.
“Let them quit,” Torres-Palma said. “They should have never played the game.”
That swagger only works if the product backs it up.
So far, Pawn Shop has a legitimate argument that it does.
Its biggest advantage might actually be the food. Pawn Shop feels less like somebody dressed up a sports bar as a restaurant than somebody built a serious restaurant and happened to cover it in televisions.
Customers can tell their server which game they want and staff can route it in seconds to televisions near their table. If someone wants USC football on one screen, the Dodgers on another, Texas football on a third and the U.S. Open nearby, you can get all of them and more at the snap of a finger.
During NFL Sundays, the two massive central media walls can even show different games, effectively splitting the room into competing fan bases.
“A lot of bars in L.A., we’re learning, don’t put the sound on,” Torres-Palma said. “We will fully lean in to actually having the sound on.”
It seems laughably obvious for a sports bar to play the sound of the game they’re featuring.
That’s also the point.
Pawn Shop is betting there’s a hole in Los Angeles between the neighborhood dive with eight televisions and mediocre wings and the actual stadium experience, where dinner can cost a fortune and nobody is going just for the cuisine.
“We are that clubhouse,” Torres-Palma said. “We just want to be a sports hub.”
And this is only phase one.
Pawn Shop plans original digital programming pairing athletes with Messina, including a concept in which the chef recreates a favorite childhood meal for a player. “Sinatra Tuesdays” are coming, featuring old-school Italian dinners and Hollywood-inspired programming. October will bring outdoor movie nights.
In February, the Super Bowl returns to Los Angeles, a time when Torres-Palma says companies are already approaching Pawn Shop about buyouts, pregame parties and postgame events.
After that?
Expansion.
“I think we’ll be opening up No. 2, or be close to opening,” Torres-Palma said of where he expects Pawn Shop to be by next summer. “Probably Vegas, almost certainly.”
For all the celebrity investors, tequila deals, televisions and franchise plans, Torres-Palma keeps coming back to something much simpler.
He wants people leaving Pawn Shop with a story to tell.
Whether that’s a World Cup goal, a Dodgers walk-off win in October, a Rams 4th quarter comeback, a chance encounter with an actor or athlete, or even a glimpse of a World Series trophy or Super Bowl ring.
“I just really want people to talk about Pawn Shop as a place where, like, ‘Oh, this crazy thing happened to me here,’” Torres-Palma said.
Ultimately, that might be Pawn Shop’s smartest bet.
L.A. has plenty of places to eat, grab a drink or watch a game.
But what Cuban, Friedman and Torres-Palma are betting their business on is that L.A. still needs a place where something worth remembering happens while you’re doing all three.

CINCINNATI (AP) — Elly De La Cruz hit a two-run homer and the Cincinnati Reds at least temporarily prevented the Los Angeles Dodgers from clinching the NL West title with a 6-2 victory on Wednesday night.
The Dodgers (92-60) needed a win or a loss by San Diego to win their fifth straight NL West crown and 13th in 14 seasons. The Padres played at Colorado later Wednesday.
Left-hander Blake Snell started for the Dodgers but departed after one inning with left groin tightness. Snell, who threw a no-hitter for the Giants in his last appearance in Great American Ball Park, faced three batters, allowing a hit with a strikeout on 19 pitches.
Blake Treinen took over in the second as the first of six relievers used by Los Angeles.
Mookie Betts singled off Andrew Abbott in the third and scored on Will Smith's double to put the Dodgers ahead 1-0. Abbott allowed a run on three hits with five walks in 4 2/3 innings. Tejay Antone (3-2), the third of six Cincinnati pitchers, got the last out of the sixth.
De La Cruz's homer off Seth Halvorsen (1-2), his 28th of the season, put the Reds ahead 2-1 in the third. It was De La Cruz's fifth longball against the Dodgers this season, most of any opposing player.
Dane Myers' homer off Bobby Miller, his seventh, extended the Reds' lead to 3-1 in the fifth.
Juan Brito's RBI single made it 4-2 in the sixth.
TJ Friedl singled with the bases loaded in the seventh to drive in two runs. Sal Stewart was thrown out at the plate by Dodgers center fielder Tommy Edman to end the inning.
The Dodgers stranded 12 runners and went 0 for 11 with runners in scoring position.
Up next
RHP Brady Singer (6-14, 5.38 ERA) will start Thursday's series finale for the Reds. The Dodgers had not announced their starter.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are looking to win their series against the Cincinnati Reds on Wednesday.
The Dodgers took Monday's series opener, 4-1, behind seven shutout innings from Tarik Skubal. Then, they won Tuesday's game, 4-0, behind seven shutout innings from Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
On Wednesday, LA has another superstar pitcher on the mound in left-hander Blake Snell.
“When you’re writing in the lineup and you see those guys, and one trying to up the other guy, and then now you got Snell going [Wednesday] — you feel good about preventing runs,” manager Dave Roberts said.
“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
Dodgers vs Reds Pitching Matchup on Wednesday
Snell is looking to continue his run of dominance since returning from midseason elbow surgery.
The left-hander has gone 4-0 with a 1.04 ERA across six starts, striking out 46 while allowing zero home runs over 34.2 innings of work.
Snell, who pitched 5.2 innings in his most recent start, is still looking to go deeper into games moving forward. He hasn't pitched more than six innings in any of his six starts.
“I mean the goal, at worst is definitely six for me,” Snell said. “I also know that I can go seven, eight, nine. I know I’m able to do it. So for me not to, I just have to get more efficient early in the game. I feel like once I get past the first couple innings, I start cruising and start figuring it out."
Opposite Snell will be left-hander Andrew Abbott, who's 6-11 with a 4.78 ERA and 120 strikeouts over 154.1 innings this season.
He's allowed seven earned runs in two of his last three starts, and has a 7.71 ERA since the start of August.

gambit – noun
a chess opening in which a player risks one or more pawns or a minor piece to gain an advantage in position
Now, if your mind immediately went to the Marvel Comics character and you were confused, fair enough. Here's the clip you likely thought of, so we can all feel better and get to the heart of the essay.
And for the record, Freddie Freeman is hardly a minor piece, but giving up a major piece for tactical advantage is called a sacrifice, which wouldn't be appropriate given the circumstances here, as Freeman returned to the lineup for the September 15 game against the Cincinnati Reds.
A funny thought occurred to me while watching Freddie Freeman these last few months:
"Where did his power go? He sure seems like he's hitting into more double plays than I remember."
Looking at Freeman's stats for the year, apart from the power and RBI numbers being down a bit, nothing looks amiss. Honestly, I originally dismissed the feeling that something was wrong because Freeman was hitting up a storm for about a month after the All-Star Break.
There wasn't much power behind it, but when someone has a slash line of .367/.402/.411 over 24 games starting from the All-Star Break, pointing out fault feels like searching for a fly in the ointment. Yes, Freeman only had four doubles, eight RBIs, and nearly three times as many strikeouts as walks, but the overall body of work looked pretty good.
Freeman had a solid couple of games in Denver where he hit for doubles power and used the entire field. However, since the Denver series, where Freeman was hitting for average, he's just not.
When you aren't hitting for either average or power, alarm bells tend to finally ring.
Power drained
On September 9, Freeman was kept out of the lineup for right knee soreness and was considered day-to-day. To his credit, Dave Roberts did mention Freeman's slump on September 9.
Roberts said there was no one incident that caused Freeman's knee soreness, but he believes it has impacted his performance at the plate lately.
"Freddie does a really good job of hitting against his front side, and then when you can't do that with your front side, your right knee, then you're compromised," Roberts said. "I see there's a lot more swing-and-miss the last few days. That's just not who he is."
In the 18 games since the Colorado series until the start of play on September 15, Freeman has a slash line of .215/.338/.292. He does have his only home run of the second half, and his strikeouts-to-walk ratio is about 1.5/1 instead of 3/1 earlier in the year.
The problem is more of the eye test: Freeman is starting to finally look, and maybe move, like his age.
The splits on Baseball Savant from last year to now tell a pretty glaring tale: if you want to beat Freeman in 2026, go low and in. Also, Freeman feasted on center-cut pitches last year, not so this year.
I'm not a hitting expert, but having a diminished knee would make it harder to rotate to hit stuff middle in. On the September 13 broadcast of the finale against the Miami Marlins, Dontrelle Willis pointed out how Freeman is compromised rotationally generally, as pitches he would normally drive the other way are being weakly hit.
Even after Freeman hit a career-high and now league-high in double plays on Sunday, the Dodgers are not seriously entertaining putting Freeman on the injured list, per Katie Woo of The Athletic:
"I think it's one of those things where we've got to manage it … just pick spots to give him an off day here or there," Roberts said. "Again, we've just got to make sure he's at optimal health when we finish the season. So I think that he might not love it, but giving him a day off here or there might be beneficial."
The Dodgers don't believe an IL stint is necessary. Instead, Roberts is working in frequent off days. That's rare for Freeman, who hasn't played in fewer than 147 games in any season as a Dodger. Freeman had a scheduled day off over the Dodgers' previous nine-game homestand and also served as the designated hitter twice in that span. He wasn't in the lineup in the last game of the homestand on Wednesday, and following a team travel day, he also sat out Friday's game.
[Emphasis added.]
Freeman insists he feels fine.
Freeman hitting into two double plays and having a key miscue that contributed to the season and series loss to the Miami Marlins seems to indicate otherwise. It's worth noting that Freeman hit another tailor-made ground ball to second on a pitcher's pitch in his final at-bat that likely would have turned into another double play had Mookie Betts not doubled earlier in the frame.
"Just talking to him today, he said he felt good," Roberts said. "Obviously, the swings don't indicate that, don't validate that. On the defense, he's obviously not moving as well as he's used to.
"I think that he's doing anything and everything he can to prepare. But yeah, the last week, it's pretty obvious that he's not himself in the box."
Freeman won't be in Monday's starting lineup, Roberts said, but should play Tuesday…
[Emphasis added.]
Much like the sense one had when watching the Americanized remake of the original 1954 classic Gojira, Godzilla: King of the Monsters, one would expect a sense of deja vu right now, even with character actor Raymond Burr long dead.
Japanese Original, American Remake
I am typically not one to mince words, and I shall not do so here. Along with Dustin Nosler of Dodgers Digest, I was dead on the money regarding the Dodgers' malpractice in not acting decisively on Ohtani and his reluctance to admit injury in the face of personal dogma of success.
I argued that the Dodgers had bungled spectacularly, and events worked themselves out to prove my initial hypothesis correct on all fronts. Now the team has backed itself into a corner regarding Ohtani.
Contrary to what some might think, I did not enjoy being right. Frankly, I am correct often enough that I do not need the constant validation, unless it comes from either the Dodgers broadcast team or national media. (In which case, gimme.)
On September 11, Katie Woo of The Athletic wrote an op-ed recently that pulled few punches:
Nobody is blameless in the Shohei Ohtani injury saga. Not the Los Angeles Dodgers' front office, which should have been more proactive in protecting the team's biggest star. Not Ohtani, who downplayed the severity of his symptoms. And while hindsight is always 20-20, there were warning signs throughout the last few weeks that suggested a stint on the injured list was the safest course of action if the organization wanted to give its prized star the best possible chance at healing in time to begin the Dodgers' quest to win three straight World Series.
As the Dodgers prepare to be without Ohtani until Sept. 23 at the earliest, their biggest concern has become a reality. When Ohtani — who is expected to be placed on the injured list on Friday — does return, there is no guarantee he'll be in optimal condition for the postseason.
[Emphasis added.]
Um, excuse me? To quote one of the finest bits of media from the 2010s, I get to channel Chris Taylor for once and declare the following:
I know, Ms. Woo means nobody relevant, but words matter, and any excuse for referential comedy is a good one.
"I think that if it were a postseason game tomorrow, (Ohtani) would be in the lineup," manager Dave Roberts said Wednesday afternoon, hours before announcing Ohtani would be placed on the IL. "I think that now you're talking about two weeks, 14 days. I feel that that's substantial. He'll be in a much better place than he was today. Is it going to be to 100 percent? Probably not. But I do think that with this time that we're taking now he'll be in an adequate spot to finish the season."
Adequate is a far cry from healthy. It is fair to question how Ohtani was handled in the second half. Should he have attempted a pitching comeback, knowing his physical health was limited? Should the Dodgers have stopped that push sooner, or placed him on the injured list earlier? In their first season of managing Ohtani as a full-season two-way player, there was always going to be some trial and error. That was acknowledged from the start of the season by both Roberts and president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman. And in fairness, there was a cognizant effort to keep Ohtani as rested as possible, including a season-long six-man rotation and an attempt to maneuver Ohtani's starts to line up on games prior to a team off day, when possible.
Hindsight is generally 20/20. I am sure if the Dodgers were armed with foreknowledge in a do-over, they would not have Ohtani's best pitching starts of the year be in Houston and San Francisco … in May.
At the risk of retreading previously covered ground, we shall conclude this portion with Roberts' regret, especially considering that Ohtani tweaked his arm in his last played game and did not immediately tell anyone about it:
Looking back, it is something Roberts wish happened a week ago.
"I think if we look right now, here today, I would love to go back and put him on the IL," the manager said. "But I did feel at that moment in time, we all felt that giving him four days was sufficient. He was agreeable. Getting him out there on Monday with the hope that he would be able to play tonight. But where we're at right now, sure."
The Dodgers should have followed their own advice or learned from their handling of Ohtani to send Freeman back to Los Angeles for ten days before arriving in Cincinnati.
They didn't.
The Dodgers have calculated that whatever value Freeman can generate in the waning days of the season is greater than the potential benefit of having Freeman recuperate for ten days, having three days against the already-eliminated San Francisco Giants to use as a tune-up. Hence, the title of this essay: the Freeman Gambit.
Yesterday's game showed promise, even with a couple of moments that made one grimace. Freeman talked about how his three-hit performance likely ensured he would play on September 16.
Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic reported Roberts' comments on the health issues of players like Ohtani, Freeman, and Edgardo Henriquez after the Dodgers clinched their fourteenth consecutive postseason appearance:
"I think right now it's front of mind, it's not great," Roberts said. "But I will say this: Once you get to October, athletes have a magical way of feeling better. It happens every single year, where there's that extra adrenaline that athletes get when you get to the postseason."
The Dodgers still boast what is likely baseball's most talented roster and an established track record of postseason success that might be enough to make history. That was the heart of Roberts' toast: that the Dodgers have not yet played their best baseball.
They still can.
"We just haven't really gotten everyone all synced up at the same time," Muncy said. "So it is a scary thought to think what we could possibly do if we did that. So hopefully that's still ahead for us at the right time."
Whether the Freeman Gambit pays off over the next two weeks before the upcoming postseason tournament is an open question. Gambits are risky, even when they work.

Mookie Betts and Kiké Hernández wore No. 21 Los Angeles Dodgers jerseys against the Cincinnati Reds on Tuesday night as part of Major League Baseball celebrating Roberto Clemente Day, which is observed every Sept. 15.
MLB permits nominees and previous recipients of the Roberto Clemente Award to wear a No. 21 jersey, and Betts was the winner of last year’s honor. Puerto Rican natives are also allowed to wear the number in honor of Clemente, which Hernández again took advantage of.
Will Smith is the Dodgers’ nominee for this year’s Roberto Clemente Award, and while he did not play in the team’s 4-0 win over the Reds, it also appears he didn’t elect to wear No. 21. Both Betts’ and Hernández’s transaction pages listed them as wearing the number, while Smith’s page still showed him wearing his usual No. 16.
Betts went 0-for-4 with a strikeout against the Reds. Hernández, like Smith, did not appear in the Dodgers’ victory.
The Roberto Clemente Award is presented annually in recognition of the Major League player who best represents the game of baseball through extraordinary character, community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions, both on and off the field.
The concept of honoring Major League players for their philanthropic work was created in 1971 as the “Commissioner’s Award.” The recognition was renamed to the “Roberto Clemente Award” in 1973 as tribute to Clemente following his passing while delivering relief supplies for earthquake victims in Nicaragua on Dec. 31, 1972.
“I was obviously too young to remember Roberto Clemente, but from the people that I respect and what he was as a person, certainly supersedes what he was as a ballplayer, which says a lot,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said on SportsNet LA.
“Just unfortunately way too young. It’s very cool that young players, current players, understand who Roberto Clemente was and they have that award every year. It’s a big feather in everyone’s cap. Baseball is certainly better with Roberto Clemente.
“I met his family in Pittsburgh, so that was pretty cool. Been to the Roberto Clemente museum in Pittsburgh, which was great for me as well.”
How to vote Will Smith for Roberto Clemente Award
Fans can now vote for the Roberto Clemente Award winner via MLBTogether.com/clementeaward (in both English and Spanish). Fan voting extends through the final day of the regular season on Sunday, Sept. 27. The winner of the fan vote will count as one vote among those cast by the blue-ribbon panel.
The league-wide winner of the Roberto Clemente Award will be honored at the 2026 World Series following selection by the aforementioned panel. It includes representatives from the commissioner’s office, Capital One, MLB-affiliated networks (MLB Network, FOX Sports, ESPN and TBS), MLB.com, National Baseball Hall of Fame, as well as Roberto’s children, Enrique, Luis and Roberto Clemente, Jr.
Smith is looking to become the fifth player in Dodgers franchise history to win the honor. Previous recipients include Betts (2025), Justin Turner (2022), Clayton Kershaw (2012) and Steve Garvey (1981).

Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman has been battling right knee pain, but the worst of it may be behind the team’s contact specialist.
Entering Tuesday’s game, Freeman was on a 3-for-30 cold streak and had missed three of the last six games because of his knee issue.
Things looked shaky for Freeman, who has built a reputation as one of baseball’s most consistent players.
However, he put together his best game in weeks, going 3-for-5 on singles, but showing the elite bat-to-ball skills that make him a candidate to bat around .300 year in, year out.
After the game, manager Dave Roberts noted that Freeman looked more like himself.
“It looked good,” Roberts said. “It looked more like Freddie.”
Freeman had asked Roberts before the game, jokingly, if he could play on Wednesday, a scheduled day off, if he got three hits.
As a result of Freeman’s performance, the manager is allowing Freeman to skip an off-day on Wednesday and play again, with the infielder eager to get the ball rolling.
“I feel like my faults are I try to hit the ball to the opposite field too much, and I let the ball get too deep,” he said.
“So today was [get the] foot down early, catch the ball out front a little bit, and it kind of worked. I wasn’t squaring the ball up in the game, but I’ll take those three hits and keep that work going tomorrow, and hopefully we’ll get hot.”
What does Freeman’s uptick mean for the Dodgers?
With the best rotation in baseball, the Dodgers are left scrounging around for offense any way that they can find it.
Teoscar Hernandez, Josue De Paula, and Mookie Betts have been the most consistent sources, with Max Muncy and Will Smith in the picture as well.
Still, the Dodgers need as many players in a spot as possible to deliver timely hits, and Freeman’s experience and skills make him a clear-cut candidate to step up.
To deliver results quickly, as he manages his knee and struggles, Freeman has made a mechanical change, getting out in front of the ball to catch it earlier on his bat.
The result may be less clean contact and hard hits, but more consistent contact, with the idea that it makes him valuable come the postseason.
“I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable,” he said. “I’m trying to find something that works for four weeks.”
Freeman has the right approach to deliver just what the Dodgers need. The entire offense does not need to be excellent; simply being good enough will lead to a three-peat.

CINCINNATI — Josue De Paula is in his element in the batter’s box. He carries himself like a guy who knows his importance to the Los Angeles Dodgers depends on how well he can command himself within those 24 square feet of chalk lines. De Paula asserts himself with a confident shake of the head after each pitch outside the strike zone.
Advertisement
Some head shakes are more exaggerated than others. Each demonstrates the same message: De Paula is not going to give in.
“I just want to feel saucy when I’m up there, you know what I’m saying?” De Paula told The Athletic this week. “I feel like I’m in control, not you. … I want my pitch. Come in the zone. Let’s go.”
This is who De Paula wants to be. He describes hitting as “aggressive patience,” an approach that puts him on the attack.
“It’s almost like a war for me in my head,” De Paula said. “I look confident. I look saucy. I feel saucy when I’m in the box, so it’s like, ‘Hey bro, let’s keep it rocking.’”
It took four games for De Paula to inspire fascination within the Dodgers dynasty, where his every at-bat feels like a must-watch example of how to command a zone. Of the first 37 big-league pitches De Paula saw outside of the strike zone, he swung at just five. He made it 17 plate appearances without striking out before going down swinging in the seventh inning and looking in the ninth in the Dodgers’ 4-0 win over the Reds on Tuesday. De Paula does not seem fazed that he is just 2 for 14 (.143) since being called up, including five hitless at-bats in his first game in the leadoff spot.
That’s because he believes in his process. A day earlier, De Paula battled back from down in the count against Reds lefty Nick Lodolo, a former All-Star. The left-handed batter took a 2-2 fastball just below the knees, crouched and shook his head. A pitch later, De Paula walked for the fifth time in his short career.
The clip of the head shake drew a chuckle from the proprietor of the “Soto Shuffle” himself, Juan Soto, who, like De Paula, once honed his craft at the El Niche Baseball Academy in the Dominican city of Santo Domingo.
Josue De Paula live reaction to you trying to get him to chase. https://t.co/CrmRSnDVgO pic.twitter.com/dbXGz8WYL0
— Chad Moriyama (@ChadMoriyama) September 14, 2026
“El loco mío,” Soto shared to his Instagram story in Spanish, stamping his approval with a laughing emoji. My guy.
Advertisement
“I swear I wasn’t trying to do like the whole thing,” De Paula said with a laugh. “I just got into my legs, and I was shaking my head … but I’m not mad. That’s not a bad player to look like.”
De Paula, 21, feels like an injection of youthful exuberance for baseball’s oldest lineup. The Brooklyn-born son of a Dominican father (and relative of NBA veterans Stephon Marbury and Sebastian Telfair) speaks with a thick New York accent and oozes the confidence of a player who carries that swagger into the box.
De Paula is the crown jewel of a Dodgers farm system that is expected to prolong this run of excellence. Last week, he became the first position player ever to be called up directly from Double A by this Andrew Friedman-led front office group.
De Paula is here because he can hit, has always hit, and the Dodgers need him to hit. De Paula is here to serve as the Dodgers’ designated hitter, at least until Shohei Ohtani returns from the injured list. No one with the Dodgers, however, is ruling out the possibility that De Paula could help them in October as they seek a third consecutive World Series title.
“I hope he makes our decision hard,” manager Dave Roberts said.
Through De Paula’s torrid run through the Dodgers’ farm system, officials raved about his keen ability to pick up the baseball, make proper swing decisions and recognize spin.
“He doesn’t give away any pitches, which I love, let alone give away any at-bats,” Roberts said.
Pair that with a preternatural ability to make contact, and De Paula entered this season as one of the highly-regarded young hitters in the league. The Dodgers implemented a change to De Paula’s swing this year, lowering his hands and opening up his resulting bat path to keep the barrel in the zone longer. That has allowed him to access more power by pulling more fly balls and has made him a lethal producer at Double A.
Advertisement
De Paula slugged 27 home runs this season in Double A, more than double what he had in any of his first four professional seasons. His first hit Sunday in Miami was a mammoth upper-deck shot to right field on the kind of awe-inspiring swing that has come much more easily for De Paula than in years past.
“When all those things are kind of clicking, it’s tough for any pitcher to compete with,” hitting coach Robert Van Scoyoc said. “So it’s been very impressive so far.”
De Paula became a Dodger partially as a byproduct of the COVID-19 pandemic, which shut down the New York baseball season and prompted De Paula’s father, Josue Sr., to send him to the Dominican Republic to work at El Niche under Cristian “Niche” Batista.
“It was like stepping into a whole other world,” De Paula said.
It was there, during an offseason workout, that De Paula met Soto, who broke into the big leagues at 19 years old with the kind of swaggering command of the batter’s box that De Paula hopes to replicate. Rather than enter the amateur draft, De Paula signed directly with the Dodgers as an international amateur for a bonus of just under $400,000. De Paula estimated that, in one of his two tryouts with the organization and with several of the club’s brass in attendance, he collected nine hits in 10 at-bats.
“I killed,” De Paula said, reliving the memory as if it just happened.
He has hit ever since, ascending to the top of prospect lists. His list of star-studded admirers grew, too. After accompanying Soto in being represented by super agent Scott Boras, De Paula was asked by Boras to name some of his favorite players. De Paula selected Elly De La Cruz, who at that time was set for his first season as a breakout star for the Cincinnati Reds but was already dominating the minor leagues. Boras invited De Paula to his Newport Beach offices in Southern California after that and surprised him by bringing De La Cruz.
Advertisement
The two have remained close, working out together in the Miami area in the winters. Friday, just before he made his major-league debut against the Marlins in Miami, De Paula called De La Cruz on FaceTime. When they met up again this week in Cincinnati, they posed for a picture.
“I’m really happy for what he’s doing,” De La Cruz said.
De Paula sees a kinship between De La Cruz and Soto.
“We’re all killers,” De Paula said with a knowing smirk.
When De Paula spent his first spring training in big-league camp with the Dodgers in 2025, he quickly heard from Mookie Betts. The former Gold Glove right fielder wanted to make De Paula and fellow newcomers Zyhir Hope and Justin Dean feel welcome, so over dinner at a Phoenix-area soul food restaurant, he talked shop. When De Paula went out for early defensive work in the outfield this week, he had Roberts and Betts at different points offer some advice.
Now in a clubhouse filled with stars, De Paula said he feels at home. Whether he stays there heading into October will depend on how the rest of the regular season goes. The first few games have left a strong first impression.
“It’s a slow heartbeat,” Van Scoyoc said. “He’s not overwhelmed at all. It seemed like he picked up where he left off in Double A. … I wouldn’t say it’s surprising, but it’s just nice to see.”
Ohtani is expected to return from his nagging biceps and knee injuries by year’s end. De Paula has a lack of defensive utility at this point. While he did play in left field on Sunday, the Dodgers still want to work on getting De Paula to “value” the defensive side of the ball first, Roberts said. That means his path to the Dodgers’ postseason roster will likely be as a left-handed bat off the bench, essentially the role the club envisioned for Dalton Rushing before his most recent IL stint.
Advertisement
That decision is still up in the air, Roberts said. There will be “growing pains,” as Roberts said after Tuesday’s performance. The manager said he “didn’t love” the quality of De Paula’s at-bats. But October is a scenario De Paula feels he will be ready for.
“Especially in big moments, I feel like my mind just goes to a whole ‘nother level,” De Paula said. “Especially competing. The bigger the moment is … it’s like the more my mind hyper-focuses. So when I’m hyper-focused like that a lot, it’s dangerous.”

Elly De La Cruz is truly ascending into Tungsten Arm O'Doyle territory of late.
Monday night saw him completely destroy a baseball, one that was conservatively estimated at 457 feet as it buzzed past the power stacks in left-center field in Great American Ball Park en route to exiting the stadium altogether. It was reminiscent of the superblast he hit from the other side of the plate off Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal just a week ago, feats of strength irreplicable by just about any other sole on the planet.
The Cincinnati Reds lost last night, though. Elly's homer was their lone run in a 4-1 loss to those very same Dodgers, a loss that officially eliminated the Reds from any miracle chance at a spot in the postseason. It also sunk them to 10 full games under .500 at 70-80, and this season is rapidly deteriorating into yet another one to forget and chuck onto the scrap-heap of memories of this once proud franchise.
I digress.
Rhett Lowder has a lot to improve upon as he heads into a vital offseason for his overall development. Anything short of a rapid change of form means the Reds need to build in even more redundancy in their starting depth plans for 2027, and there's been precious little in the way of advancement from their former 1st round pick so far in his own disappointing 2026. He'll get the start tonight, while the Dodgers will counter with Yoshinobu Yamamoto.

The Los Angeles Dodgers shortstop Mookie Betts is producing a new movie. On Monday, he announced the project away from the field. He's producing a movie titled "Cannon Street All-Stars."
Los Angeles clinched a playoff berth the same day, beating the Cincinnati Reds 4-1. The win pushed them to 91-59 with 12 games left. It marks the Dodgers' 14th straight postseason appearance.
However, Betts did little to contribute to that win. He went 0-for-4. No hits, home runs or RBIs.
He is having a down year by his standards.
Betts is batting .248 with 20 home runs, 62 RBIs and 108 hits this season. His career average sits at .288. Betts won AL MVP in 2018 and has made eight All-Star teams.
Off the diamond, however, he is excelling in his projects.
More on Mookie Betts' Latest Project
Betts is producing the film alongside Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry, Deadline reported in an exclusive Monday.
Director Reggie Rock Bythewood and his wife, Gina Prince-Bythewood, are developing the project through their company, Undisputed Cinema. Bythewood will write and direct.
The film tells the true story of the Cannon Street YMCA All-Stars. The all-Black Little League team from Charleston, South Carolina, tried to enter the 1955 state tournament.
Little League baseball in the South remained segregated at the time, eight years after Jackie Robinson broke MLB's color line. The team's push sparked forfeits and national attention. The Jackie Robinson Foundation backs the project.
Bythewood called the film overdue recognition. Surviving players were honored at last year's Little League World Series. "Now it is time to honor them on film," Bythewood said.
Betts produces through his company, OMG Entertainment, alongside Cam Lewis and Omar Bradford. Curry produces through Unanimous Media with Sharla Sumpter Bridgett. Debra Martin Chase and E. Monique Floyd also produce.
Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman Latest Updates
Despite clinching the postseason, few key pieces remain uncertain.
Shohei Ohtani is on the 15-day injured list with left knee and right biceps issues. He landed there Sept. 11.
Manager Dave Roberts said Monday that Ohtani could begin swinging off a tee as early as this week. The Dodgers expect Ohtani back as a hitter in late September. He won't pitch again this season. Ohtani is batting .277 with 30 home runs and 80 RBIs this year.
Freddie Freeman sat out Monday's game to rest a sore right knee, described as patellar tendinitis. The team does not plan to place him on the injured list. Freeman is expected back in the lineup Tuesday.

MIAMI –– The Dodgers’ bullpen melted down once again on Sunday in Miami.
Only this time, they got an unhelpful hand from some shaky late-game defense.
In a 6-4 loss to the Miami Marlins, the Dodgers allowed all of the scoring in the final two innings of what became a walk-off defeat; watching three high-leverage relievers –– Edgardo Henriquez, Tanner Scott and Brock Stewart –– falter after their infield gave away extra outs behind them.
In Henriquez’s two-run eighth inning, one would-be groundout instead snuck between shortstop Mookie Betts and second baseman Miguel Rojas, leaving Rojas injured after he made a late sliding attempt. Another got stuck in Betts’ hand while he tried to make a charging throw on the run, gifting the Marlins a free scoring opportunity that would lead to a two-run single from Otto Lopez.
The four-run ninth inning, which was capped off by Agustín Ramírez’s walk-off homer against Stewart, was just as frustrating, as Scott’s bid for a four-out save imploded after a pair of infield singles; one on a bunt, and another on a bad underhand flipped from a hobbled Freddie Freeman at first base.
“When you give a team extra outs,” manager Dave Roberts said, “that’s what happens.”
Initially, it appeared as though the Dodgers might still escape.
After Lopez’s single in the eighth, Scott replaced Henriquez to face Griffin Conine and struck him out on three pitches to end the inning and keep a 3-2 lead intact.
In the top of the ninth, the Dodgers added to the advantage on Betts’ RBI double, giving them “enough to win” offensively, as Roberts put it, even though they left the bases loaded later in the frame.
Alas, the bottom of the ninth immediately went sideways on an Xavier Edwards ground ball to lead off the inning.
Freeman, who has been playing through a knee injury and is mired in a 1-for-26 slump, fielded the ball but made a bad underhand flip back to first. Scott had to adjust to it as he went to cover the base, and was too late to recover as Edwards beat the play out.
Jakob Marsee came up next and executed a perfect bunt inside the third-base line.
Then, Javier Sanoja got jammed by a slider but still muscled a two-run double into the left-field corner.
Just like that, the Dodgers’ lead was gone. It was only Scott’s fourth blown save in 26 opportunities this season, but also the sixth time in his last 11 outings he has given up a run.
“Actually, I think the last week has been really good as far as the stuff,” Roberts said when asked of that trend, which has pushed Scott’s ERA to 2.91. “Today I think was just an odd day.”
Four pitches later, the game was over. Stewart came in to face the pinch-hitting Ramírez, but grooved him a fastball that was launched to left for the walk-off blast.
“It was supposed to be up above the zone. That’s where my fastball plays best,” Stewart said. “Just missed my spot, threw it right down the middle.”
Thus, the Dodgers suffered a loss that wasted big days from Emmet Sheehan (who threw six scoreless innings in his start) and Josue De Paula (who mashed a monstrous three-run home run in the fourth inning for his first career hit), while also delaying any possibility of clinching a playoff spot for a second-straight day.
“It’s baseball,” Roberts said. “It sucks. It feels bad. But that’s part of the thing.”
With a sigh, he later added: “But yeah, today was a crappy one.”
